key_concept: In a coordination compound only the counter ions outside the coordination sphere (square brackets) ionise in water, so the electrolyte type is set by the ratio of complex ion to counter ions.
steps: A 1:3 electrolyte gives one complex ion and three counter ions per formula unit, i.e. 4 ions in total.
Option (1): $[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl \rightarrow [CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]^+ + Cl^-$ gives 2 ions, so it is a 1:1 electrolyte.
Option (2): $[CoCl(NH_3)_5]Cl_2 \rightarrow [CoCl(NH_3)_5]^{2+} + 2Cl^-$ gives 3 ions, so it is a 1:2 electrolyte.
Option (3): $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3 \rightarrow [Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+} + 3Cl^-$ gives 4 ions, so it is a 1:3 electrolyte.
Option (4): $[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]$ is a neutral complex with no counter ions, so it is a non-electrolyte.
Only option (3) is a 1:3 electrolyte, which matches the official key.
why_not_others: In options (1) and (2), some $Cl^-$ ions are bonded inside the coordination sphere as ligands and do not ionise, so these compounds give only 1:1 and 1:2 behaviour. Option (4) has no ions outside the bracket at all, so it does not conduct.
common_trap: Students count all the chlorines in the formula, including those bound to Co inside the brackets, instead of counting only the ionisable chlorides outside the bracket.
time_saving_tip: Just count the anions written outside the square brackets: three outside means a 1:3 electrolyte (this also matches 3 mol AgCl precipitated per mole with $AgNO_3$).
